course.title: Graphic Design & Visual Theory
course.shortDescription: Learn to see like a designer — line, shape, color, typography, and layout — through the acclaimed GCF Beginning Graphic Design series, with a hands-on CSS poster lab.
course.longDescription:
This showcase course builds visual literacy from first principles using the GCFGlobal Beginning Graphic Design video series. Each module pairs one complete video lesson with a deeper reading and scenario quizzes that train your eye: why one poster feels balanced and another chaotic, why some color pairs sing and others clash, and how typography sets a mood before a single word is read.

The closing lab has you apply hierarchy, contrast, and alignment in a live web canvas, and the final exam tests whether you can reason about design decisions — not just recognize terms.
course.courseSummary: Design fundamentals (line, shape, form, texture, balance), color theory (the color wheel, harmony schemes, hue/saturation/value), typography (serif/sans-serif, hierarchy, pairing), and layout & composition (proximity, white space, alignment, contrast, repetition).

content.description: Line, shape, form, texture, and balance — the raw materials every design is made of.
content.problemStatement: Line, shape, form, texture, and balance — the raw materials every design is made of.

contentBlocks.content:
Design is a language — these are its letters

Every logo, poster, and interface is assembled from the same five raw materials:

  • Line — connects, divides, directs the eye; a line's weight and texture carry mood
  • Shape — geometric (circles, squares: order, stability) vs. organic (freeform: natural, human)
  • Form — shape plus the illusion of depth: shadows, highlights, perspective
  • Texture — the suggested surface feel; adds richness but competes for attention
  • Balance — the distribution of visual weight; symmetrical feels formal, asymmetrical feels dynamic (and is harder to pull off)

Watch the video with one question in mind: when a design feels "off," which of these five is misbehaving? That diagnostic habit is the whole skill.

Train your eye today

Pick any app on your phone and identify: one deliberate use of line, the dominant shape family, and whether the layout balances symmetrically or asymmetrically. Do this daily and "designer's eye" stops being a mystery.

content.problemStatement: A poster has one large dark photo on the left and only a small headline on the far right; the whole composition feels like it is tipping over. Which principle is being violated?

content.description: The color wheel, harmony schemes, and the three dials — hue, saturation, and value — that control every color.
content.problemStatement: The color wheel, harmony schemes, and the three dials — hue, saturation, and value — that control every color.

contentBlocks.content:
Color is a system, not a guess

Confident color choices come from the color wheel and a handful of harmony formulas:

  • Monochromatic — one hue, varied lightness: always safe, can feel flat
  • Analogous — neighbors on the wheel (blue, teal, green): harmonious, low tension
  • Complementary — opposites (blue/orange): maximum vibrance, use one as the star and one as the accent
  • Triadic — three evenly spaced hues: lively, needs careful proportion

And every individual color is three dials: hue (which color), saturation (how intense), value (how light or dark). Most "ugly" palettes fail on saturation — everything screaming at 100% — not on hue choice.

The working designer's shortcut

Pick one dominant color, one neutral, and one accent — a 60/30/10 split. Desaturate the dominant, save full saturation for the accent. This single habit produces palettes that look professional before you know why.

units.title: Type Speaks Before You Read It

content.description: Serif vs sans-serif, display faces, hierarchy, and how to pair fonts without chaos.
content.problemStatement: Serif vs sans-serif, display faces, hierarchy, and how to pair fonts without chaos.

contentBlocks.content:
Every font has a voice

Before a reader processes a single word, the letterforms have already set the tone. The three families to command:

  • Serif (small feet on the strokes — Times, Georgia): traditional, authoritative, bookish
  • Sans-serif (clean strokes — Helvetica, Inter): modern, neutral, screen-friendly
  • Display/decorative: personality fonts for headlines only — never body text

Hierarchy is typography's real job: size, weight, and spacing tell the reader what to read first, second, and last. And the classic pairing formula: one serif + one sans-serif, clearly different in role, never two near-identical fonts fighting each other.

Leading, tracking, kerning

Three spacing terms worth owning: leading (space between lines — too tight suffocates, too loose disconnects), tracking (uniform letter spacing across a word or block), and kerning (space between a specific pair of letters). Headlines almost always need manual kerning attention; body text almost never does.

content.description: Proximity, white space, alignment, contrast, and repetition — the five habits of composition.
content.problemStatement: Proximity, white space, alignment, contrast, and repetition — the five habits of composition.

contentBlocks.content:
Composition: where the pieces meet

You have elements (module 1), colors (module 2), and type (module 3). Layout is how they share the page, governed by five habits:

  • Proximity — related things sit together; unrelated things get distance
  • White space — emptiness is not waste; it is what makes the content legible and premium
  • Alignment — every element should line up with something; invisible grids create visible order
  • Contrast — differences in size, color, or weight signal importance
  • Repetition — repeating styles (same button shape, same heading color) creates unity across pages

After the video, you will apply all five in a live CSS lab.

content.title: Lab: Compose an Event Poster
content.question: Apply hierarchy, contrast, alignment, and white space to design a digital event poster in CSS.
content.description:
The unstyled content of an event poster is provided. Using CSS only, apply the course principles:

  • Hierarchy: the event title must clearly dominate (largest, boldest); date and venue secondary; details smallest
  • Contrast: a dark background with light text, plus ONE saturated accent color used only for the call-to-action
  • Alignment: all text aligned to a single axis (left or center — pick one and commit)
  • White space: generous padding and margins between groups; related lines (date + venue) sit closer together than unrelated ones
content.problemStatement: Style the provided poster markup: dominant title, secondary date/venue grouped by proximity, one accent color for the CTA only, one alignment axis, and generous white space on a dark background.
